GR00T · SONIC · Isaac Sim testbench — input diagnostic

What the VLA policy sees: sim vs. its training data

Side-by-side of the exact observations fed to bs256/checkpoint-12000 from the live Isaac Sim run, against a recorded episode from the training/eval dataset. Captured while the robot flailed regardless of prompt.

Verdict — the policy is out of distribution on two independent axes

The flailing is not (mainly) a bad checkpoint: the pipeline feeds it synthetic images where it learned from real photos, and a base orientation that reads as tipped 90°. Either alone is enough to break it.

Findings

critical

Visual sim-to-real gap

The policy was trained on real-robot camera frames (metallic arms, black gloved hands, real objects & lighting). The sim feeds synthetic Isaac Sim renders. The two ego_view images below share almost no visual statistics — this alone puts every frame out of distribution.

critical

Orientation frame mismatch

projected_gravity the policy actually receives is [0.02, −0.99, 0.13] (computed with the repo's own compute_projected_gravity) — gravity along −Y, i.e. the robot reads as tipped ~90°. Training data is [−0.03, 0.02, −1.0] (upright, −Z). A tipped-over proprioceptive signal would provoke violent “recovery” motion regardless of prompt.

mismatch

Extra camera modalities

Training used a single camera (observation.images.ego_view). The sim publishes and the client forwards left_wrist and right_wrist as well — inputs the checkpoint never trained against.

note

Undertrained checkpoint (context)

bs256/checkpoint-12000 is step 12000 of 20000, epoch 0.6. Even in-distribution it may be weak — but the two issues above dominate.
